 Layoffs and favouritism? Qualcomm’s job cuts trigger questions over fairness
 As Qualcomm’s restructuring in India unfolds, employee discussions are shifting the HR conversation from workforce optimisation to the perceived transparency and objectivity of layoff decisions. By HRK News Bureau November 19, 2026 2 Mins Read 1653 Views

 WhatsApp 
 Qualcomm’s ongoing workforce-reduction exercise in India has sparked debate over how employees were selected for layoffs, with allegations of managerial bias emerging alongside concerns about performance-linked exits. According to an analysis by workplace community platform Blind, reported by People Matters, nearly half of the discussions related to Qualcomm’s layoffs referenced workplace politics or favouritism as a factor in termination decisions.
 Blind’s AI-driven review of employee conversations found that 47.7 per cent of Qualcomm-related layoff discussions mentioned politics or favouritism, significantly higher than comparable discussions involving Meta, Microsoft and Uber. In contrast, 34.2 per cent of Qualcomm conversations focused on cost management or performance factors.
 While the findings do not establish whether bias occurred, they do indicate the dominant themes employees associated with the layoffs. Among the companies analysed, Qualcomm generated the highest proportion of conversations centred on perceived favouritism.
 India has been at the heart of these discussions, accounting for 87 per cent of Qualcomm-related layoff conversations on Blind. Employees raised concerns about managerial discretion in performance evaluations, promotions and workforce decisions. Some discussions alleged preferential treatment based on regional affiliations, language backgrounds or previous professional networks. Others questioned whether remote workers, employees on medical leave, or those returning from maternity leave faced greater vulnerability during the restructuring process.
 The concerns have surfaced as Qualcomm reportedly undertakes a major restructuring across its India operations, with reports suggesting that more than 1,000 roles could be affected. Engineering and research teams across multiple locations are expected to feel the impact, although the company has not officially confirmed the number of jobs being eliminated.
 The restructuring reportedly follows annual performance reviews and is linked to business priorities, future skill requirements and organisational realignment. Clearly, even when layoffs are positioned as performance-driven, employee trust ultimately depends on whether selection criteria are viewed as transparent, consistent and fair.
